t.6.47.3: Hearing that Prahasta had been slain in battle, he, tormented by grief, his mind overcome with wrath, spoke to those foremost of the Nairṛta warriors, just as Indra speaks to the foremost warriors of the immortals.
t.6.47.1: When that guardian of the rākṣasa army had been slain in battle by the bull among the monkeys, the army of the king of the rākṣasas, bearing fearsome weapons and with a force like that of the ocean, fled away.
t.6.47.2: Going to the lord of the rākṣasas, they reported that his commander had been struck down by the son of Pāvaka; and hearing those words of theirs, the lord of the rākṣasas fell under the sway of rage.
t.6.47.4: No contempt should be shown toward the enemy, by whom my army commander, the crusher of Indra's forces, has been slain together with his retinue and his elephant.
t.6.47.5: Therefore I myself, without hesitation, will go to that wondrous forefront of battle for the destruction of the enemies and for victory.
t.6.47.6: Today I shall burn up that army of monkeys, and Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa, with floods of arrows, as blazing fires burn up a forest.
t.6.47.7: Having spoken thus, the enemy of the king of the immortals mounted his chariot, which shone like fire, was yoked with teams of the finest horses, and glowed and blazed with its splendid form.
t.6.47.8: Then that foremost king of the rākṣasas set forth, honored with the blare of conches, kettledrums and war-drums, with the slapping of arms, shrill cries and lion-like roars, and with auspicious hymns of praise.
t.6.47.9: Surrounded by the foremost of the rākṣasa chiefs, flesh-eaters whose forms were like mountains and clouds and whose eyes blazed like fire, he shone like Rudra, lord of the immortals, surrounded by the bhūtas.
t.6.47.10: Then the mighty one, swiftly going forth from the city, saw that fierce army of monkeys, roaring like the great ocean and the thunderclouds, poised for battle with trees and rocks in their hands.
t.6.47.11: Beholding that exceedingly fierce host of rākṣasas, Rāma of great splendour, whose arms were like the lord of serpents, followed by his army, spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa, the foremost of those who bear weapons.
t.6.47.12: Whose is this unshakable army, thronged with banners, standards and weapons of many kinds, bristling with lances, swords, spears, missiles and discuses, crowded with elephants like the lords of mountains, and manned by fearless warriors?
t.6.47.13: Then, having heard Rāma's words, Vibhīṣaṇa, equal in valour to Śakra, described to Rāma the foremost of the forces of those great-souled bulls among the Rākṣasas.
t.6.47.14: That great-souled one who rides upon the elephant's shoulder, his face coppery like the newly risen sun, and who approaches making the elephant's head sway, know him to be Akampana, O king.
t.6.47.15: That one standing in his chariot with a lion on his banner, brandishing a bow that gleams like Indra's bow, who shines like an elephant with fierce, protruding tusks, is the one named Indrajit, pre-eminent through the boons he has won.
t.6.47.16: And this one who resembles the Vindhya, Asta and Mahendra mountains, a bowman standing in his chariot, a peerless chariot-warrior of surpassing valour, twanging his bow of matchless size, is Atikāya by name, whose body is exceedingly vast.
t.6.47.17: That one there, with eyes copper-red like the newly risen sun, who has mounted an elephant resounding with the ringing of bells and roars harshly, that great-souled one is the hero named Mahodara.
t.6.47.18: That one who, mounted on a horse with variegated golden trappings that shines like a mountain of evening clouds, brandishes a lance wreathed in rays of light, is Piśāca, swift as the thunderbolt.
t.6.47.20: And that one there, whose form resembles a rain-cloud, is Kumbha, with a broad, expansive and well-formed chest; composed and bearing the king of serpents on his banner, he shines as he stretches and brandishes his bow.
t.6.47.19: And this one who comes grasping a sharp spear that gleams like lightning and has the speed of the Kiṃkaras' thunderbolt, mounted on a lordly bull that looks like a mountain, is the illustrious Triśiras.
t.6.47.21: And he who comes this way grasping a blazing, smoking iron club studded with gold and diamonds, standing as the very banner of the Rākṣasa host, that one is Nikumbha, whose deeds are wondrous and terrible.
t.6.47.22: And he who, mounted on a bannered chariot furnished with masses of bows, swords and arrows, its form blazing like fire, shines forth towering high, that is Narāntaka, who fights with mountain peaks.
t.6.47.24: Where that foremost white parasol with fine ribs shines, resembling the moon, there this great-souled lord of the Rākṣasas, surrounded by beings, appears radiant like Rudra.
t.6.47.23: And this one who shines forth, surrounded by beings of many kinds and terrible forms, with the faces of tigers, camels, lordly elephants and lions, and with rolling eyes, he is the one who crushes the pride even of the gods.
t.6.47.25: That one, crowned, his face lit by swaying earrings, his body as fearsome as the lord of elephants or the Vindhya mountains, the crusher of the pride of Mahendra and Vaivasvata, the lord of the Rākṣasas, shines like the sun.
t.6.47.26: Then Rāma replied to Vibhīṣaṇa, the subduer of foes: "Ah, how blazing is Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, endowed with great splendor!"
t.6.47.28: Even the heroes among the gods and Dānavas could not possess such a form as this form of the lord of the Rākṣasas that now shines forth.
t.6.47.29: His warriors, of great might, are all like mountains, all fight with mountains, and all bear blazing weapons.
t.6.47.30: That king of the Rākṣasas shines forth, surrounded by blazing, fierce beings of terrible valour, like Antaka, Death himself, surrounded by embodied spirits.
t.6.47.31: Having spoken thus, the valiant Rāma then took up his bow and, drawing out an excellent arrow, stood ready, with Lakṣmaṇa following him.
t.6.47.32: Then that great-souled lord of the rākṣasas said to those mighty rākṣasas: "Stand at the gates, at the watch-houses and at the gate-towers, fully at ease and free from all apprehension."
t.6.47.27: Like the sun, Rāvaṇa shines with his rays, hard to look upon; for I clearly perceive his form enveloped in radiant splendour.
t.6.47.33: Then, having swiftly dismissed them, and the rākṣasas having gone according to their orders, he tore through the ocean-like flood of monkeys, as a great sea-monster tears through the brimming flood of the sea.
t.6.47.34: Seeing that lord of the rākṣasas rushing swiftly upon him in battle, his bow and arrows blazing, the lord of the monkeys tore up a great mountain peak and charged at the overlord of the rākṣasas.
t.6.47.35: Seizing that mountain peak, its slopes thick with many trees, he hurled it at the night-roamer; but the other, seeing it suddenly hurtling toward him, shattered it with arrows fletched with gold.
t.6.47.37: Enraged, he seized that arrow, swift as the wind, blazing like a fire with flying sparks, its speed equal to great Indra's thunderbolt, and hurled it to slay Sugrīva.
t.6.47.36: When that peak, its excellent slopes covered with tall trees, had been shattered and had fallen to the earth, the lord of the world of the rākṣasas took up an arrow that was like a mighty serpent and resembled Death itself.
t.6.47.39: Afflicted by the arrows, his mind confounded, the hero fell to the earth, moaning. Seeing him fallen senseless on the ground, the yātudhānas roared in delight on the battlefield.
t.6.47.38: That sharp-pointed arrow, released from Rāvaṇa's arm and shaped like Śakra's thunderbolt, reached Sugrīva and pierced him with great force, just as the fierce spear hurled by Guha pierced Mount Krauñca.
t.6.47.40: Then Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Sudaṃṣṭra, and likewise Ṛṣabha, Jyotirmukha and Nala, their bodies grown huge, lifted up mountains and rushed toward that lord of the rākṣasas.
t.6.47.42: Those monkey-lords of terrible form, pierced by the arrows of the enemy of the gods, fell upon the ground. Then he covered that fierce monkey army with nets of arrows.
t.6.47.41: With hosts of sharp-tipped arrows the lord of the rākṣasas turned their blows into mere clouds, and with volleys of arrows whose shafts were brightly adorned with gold he pierced those lords of the vānaras as well.
t.6.47.43: Being slaughtered, their foremost heroes fallen, screaming again and again, pierced by the darts of fear and tormented by Rāvaṇa's arrows, those monkeys went to Rāma, the giver of refuge, for refuge.
t.6.47.44: Then the great-souled Rāma, the bowman, took up his bow and set out at once. Lakṣmaṇa approached him with joined palms and spoke words full of the highest purpose.
t.6.47.45: Certainly, noble one, you are fully able to slay this evil-souled wretch, yet I shall destroy the vile one myself; grant me leave, O lord.
t.6.47.46: To him spoke Rāma of great splendour, whose valour was true: "Go, Lakṣmaṇa, and be ever intent on striving in the battle."
t.6.47.47: For Rāvaṇa is of great valor and of wondrous prowess in battle; when enraged, he cannot be withstood even by the three worlds, of this there is no doubt.
t.6.47.48: Seek out his weak points and guard your own; with eye and bow, carefully and with a collected mind, protect yourself.
t.6.47.49: Having heard the words of Rāghava, Saumitri embraced him and honoured him; then, having saluted Rāma, he went forth to battle.
t.6.47.51: Seeing him, the greatly radiant Hanūmān, son of the Wind-god, warded off the volleys of arrows and rushed at Rāvaṇa.
t.6.47.50: He, whose arms were like an elephant's trunk, saw Rāvaṇa, his terrible bow blazing and raised, covering those monkeys with nets of showering arrows, their bodies pierced and scattered about.
t.6.47.52: Approaching his chariot and raising his right arm, the wise Hanūmān, terrifying Rāvaṇa, spoke these words.
t.6.47.53: Being unslayable, you have crushed the Devas, Dānavas and Gandharvas, and the Yakṣas together with the Rākṣasas; but from the monkeys there is danger for you.
t.6.47.54: This right arm of mine, five-fingered and raised up, will drive out from your body the living soul that has long dwelt there.
t.6.47.55: Having heard the words of Hanūmān, Rāvaṇa of terrible prowess, his eyes reddened with anger, spoke these words.
t.6.47.56: Strike quickly and without fear, and win lasting fame; then I shall destroy you, O monkey, valiant among your kin.
t.6.47.58: Thus addressed, the greatly radiant and mighty Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, struck the son of the Wind on the chest with the palm of his hand.
t.6.47.57: Having heard Rāvaṇa's words, the son of Vāyu spoke these words: "Remember your son Akṣa, who was struck down by me before."
t.6.47.59: Struck by him with the palm of the hand, he staggered again and again; then, greatly enraged, he struck the enemy of the gods with his palm in return.
t.6.47.60: Then, struck by the great-souled monkey with the palm of his hand, Daśagrīva was violently shaken, like a mountain during an earthquake.
t.6.47.61: Seeing Rāvaṇa thus struck by the palm of a hand in battle, the Ṛṣis, the Vānaras, the Siddhas, and the Devas together with the Asuras cried out aloud.
t.6.47.62: Then the greatly splendid Rāvaṇa, having recovered his breath, spoke these words: “Well done, O monkey! By your valour you are a foe worthy of my praise.”
t.6.47.63: Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, Māruti spoke these words: "Shame on my valour, that you still live, O Rāvaṇa!"
t.6.47.64: "Strike me just once now, O wicked-minded one, why do you boast? Then my fist will lead you to the abode of Yama." Then, at the words of Māruti, his anger blazed up.
t.6.47.66: Then, seeing the mighty Hanūmān staggered, the great chariot-warrior swiftly advanced in his chariot toward Nīla.
t.6.47.65: His eyes reddened with rage, the mighty one raised his right fist with effort and brought it down with force upon the monkey's chest. Struck in turn on his broad chest, Hanumān reeled.
t.6.47.67: With dreadful arrows like serpents, which pierced deep into the vitals of foes, he set ablaze Nīla, the commander of the monkey army.
t.6.47.68: Nīla, commander of the monkey army, though sorely afflicted by the flood of arrows, hurled a mountain peak with one hand at the lord of the Rākṣasas.
t.6.47.69: The glorious and great-minded Hanūmān, too, having recovered his breath and looking about, eager for battle, angrily spoke these words.
t.6.47.70: Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, is engaged in combat with Nīla; it is not proper to rush upon one who is fighting with another.
t.6.47.71: Rāvaṇa too, of great splendour, struck that mountain peak with seven very sharp-pointed arrows, and it fell, shattered to pieces.
t.6.47.72: Seeing that mountain peak scattered to pieces, the commander of the monkey army, slayer of enemy heroes, blazed with rage like the fire at the end of time.
t.6.47.73: In the battle, Nīla hurled aśvakarṇa trees, dhava trees, sāla trees, and mango trees in full bloom, and many other kinds of trees as well.
t.6.47.74: Rāvaṇa, encountering those trees, cut them to pieces, and he rained down upon Pāvaki a most dreadful shower of arrows.
t.6.47.75: Showered by a flood of arrows as a great mountain is by a rain-cloud, he then made his form small and dropped down onto the top of the flagstaff.
t.6.47.76: Seeing the son of Pāvaka stationed on the top of his banner, Rāvaṇa blazed with rage, and then Nīla roared.
t.6.47.78: Rāvaṇa too, of great splendour, astonished at the monkey's swiftness, called forth a wondrous, blazing missile of Agni.
t.6.47.77: Seeing that monkey perched on the top of the flagstaff, on the tip of the bow, and on the top of the crown, Lakṣmaṇa, Hanumān and Rāma were amazed.
t.6.47.79: Then those monkeys, delighted at having found their chance, shouted aloud when they saw Rāvaṇa in the battle bewildered by Nīla's nimbleness.
t.6.47.80: Then Rāvaṇa, enraged by the roaring of the monkeys, his heart seized with agitation, could not decide on anything at all.
t.6.47.81: Then Rāvaṇa, the night-roamer, taking up an arrow joined with the fire-weapon, looked up at Nīla, who stood upon the top of his banner.
t.6.47.82: Then the greatly radiant Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, said: "O monkey, by this supreme māyā of yours you are endowed with swiftness."
t.6.47.84: Even so, the arrow released by me and charged with the power of a divine weapon will strip you of your life, though you strive to guard it.
t.6.47.83: Save your life, indeed, if you can, O monkey, you who create these various forms of yourself again and again.
t.6.47.85: Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, fitted an arrow charged with a divine weapon and struck the commander of the army.
t.6.47.86: Struck in the chest by an arrow charged with a divine weapon, Nīla, being consumed by fire, suddenly fell to the surface of the earth.
t.6.47.88: Seeing the monkey senseless, Daśagrīva, eager for battle, rushed at Saumitri in his chariot that roared like a thundercloud.
t.6.47.87: Through his connection with his father's greatness, and also by his own fiery energy, he fell to the ground on his knees, yet he was not parted from his life-breaths.
t.6.47.89: To him, as he was stretching his immeasurable bow, Saumitri of undaunted spirit said: "Come after me alone, O lord of the night-roamers; you ought not to fight against the monkeys."
t.6.47.90: Hearing his words, full and resounding, and the fierce twang of his bowstring, that king of the rākṣasas approached Saumitri, who stood there filled with anger, and spoke these words.
t.6.47.91: By good fortune, Rāghava, you of perverse mind, bound for your end, have come within the path of my sight! At this very moment you will go to the realm of death, overwhelmed by the nets of my arrows.
t.6.47.92: To him, roaring with his white-tipped fangs bared, Saumitri, unperturbed, said: "O king, those of great might do not roar; yet you boast, O foremost of evildoers."
t.6.47.94: Thus addressed, the lord of the rākṣasas, enraged, loosed seven well-feathered arrows; Lakṣmaṇa cut them down with arrows whose feathers were bright with gold and whose points were keenly sharpened.
t.6.47.93: I know your valor, O lord of the Rākṣasas, your strength, your splendor and your prowess. I stand here with bow and arrows in hand; come on! What use is this empty boasting?
t.6.47.96: But he, Rāma's younger brother, rained down a fierce shower of arrows loosed from his bow, and with razor-headed, crescent-headed, excellent barbed and broad-headed arrows he cut down the arrows of his foe, and he was not shaken.
t.6.47.95: Seeing those arrows suddenly cut down, like lordly serpents with their coils severed, the lord of Laṅkā fell under the sway of anger and loosed other sharpened arrows.
t.6.47.97: And Lakṣmaṇa swiftly fitted to his bow sharp-pointed arrows, blazing like fire and swift as the thunderbolt of great Indra, and loosed them for the slaying of the lord of the rākṣasas.
t.6.47.98: The lord of the rākṣasas cut those arrows to pieces, and having cut them, he struck Lakṣmaṇa on the forehead with an arrow given by Svayambhū, blazing like the fire of universal destruction.
t.6.47.99: Lakṣmaṇa, stricken by Rāvaṇa's arrows, staggered, holding his bow loosely; then, regaining consciousness with difficulty, he cut through the bow of the foe of the lord of the thirty gods.
t.6.47.101: His bow cut asunder and himself struck by arrows, his limbs drenched with sweat and smeared with blood, that enemy of the gods, of towering might, seized in battle the spear that Svayambhū had given him.
t.6.47.100: Then Dāśarathi struck him, whose bow had been cut, with three sharp-pointed arrows. Afflicted by the arrows, the king reeled, and only with difficulty did he regain consciousness.
t.6.47.102: That lord of the rākṣasa realm swiftly hurled at Saumitri that blazing spear, which resembled a smokeless fire and struck terror into the monkey hosts.
t.6.47.103: As it came hurtling toward him, Bharata's younger brother struck at it with missiles and with arrows like sacrificial fire into which oblations have been poured; yet even so, that spear pierced the broad chest of Dāśarathi.
t.6.47.104: Struck in the middle of the chest by the Brahmā-given spear, Saumitri recalled himself to be his own inconceivable portion of Viṣṇu.
t.6.47.105: Then the thorn of the gods, having crushed Saumitri, the destroyer of the Dānavas' pride, with his two arms, was powerless to move him.
t.6.47.107: Then, seeing Lakṣmaṇa, that portion of Viṣṇu who had taken on a human body, lying unconscious, Rāvaṇa was astonished.
t.6.47.106: Himavat, Mandara, Meru, or even the three worlds together with the immortals could be lifted with his two arms, but not Bharata's younger brother on the battlefield.
t.6.47.108: Then the enraged son of Vāyu rushed at Rāvaṇa, and in his fury he struck him on the chest with a fist like a thunderbolt.
t.6.47.109: Struck by that blow of the fist, Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, sank to the ground on his knees; he reeled and fell.
t.6.47.111: The mighty Hanūmān too, taking Lakṣmaṇa, who had been struck down by Rāvaṇa, in his two arms, carried him to the side of Rāghava.
t.6.47.110: Seeing Rāvaṇa of terrible prowess lying senseless in battle, the seers and the monkeys, and the gods together with Vāsava, cried out aloud.
t.6.47.113: Having released Saumitri, invincible in battle, that śakti returned once more to its place in Rāvaṇa's chariot.
t.6.47.112: Because of the friendship and supreme devotion of the son of Vāyu, he, though immovable by his enemies, became light for the monkey.
t.6.47.114: Rāvaṇa too, of great splendor, having regained consciousness in the great battle, took up sharpened arrows and seized his mighty bow.
t.6.47.115: Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of foes, revived and freed from the arrow's shaft, recalling that he himself was an inscrutable portion of Viṣṇu.
t.6.47.116: But Rāghava, seeing on the battlefield the great army of the monkeys with its mighty heroes struck down, rushed upon Rāvaṇa.
t.6.47.117: Then Hanūmān approached him and spoke these words: "Mount upon my back, and you should chastise the Rākṣasa."
t.6.47.118: Hearing those words spoken by the son of Vāyu, the heroic Rāghava at once mounted Hanūmān, the great monkey. Then the lord of men beheld Rāvaṇa standing in his chariot on the battlefield.
t.6.47.119: Seeing him, that greatly radiant Rāghava rushed toward him, like the enraged Viṣṇu with weapon upraised charging at Vairocana.
t.6.47.120: He made a fierce twang of the bowstring, resounding like the crash of a thunderbolt, and in a deep voice Rāma spoke to the lord of the Rākṣasas.
t.6.47.121: Stay, stay! For having done me such a wrong, where can you go, O tiger among rākṣasas, and find release?
t.6.47.122: Even if you go to Indra, Vaivasvata or Bhāskara, or to Svayambhū, Vaiśvānara or Śaṃkara, or flee into the ten directions, even so, now that you have come within my reach, you will not escape me today.
t.6.47.124: Having heard the words of Rāghava, the lord of the Rākṣasas struck the great monkey with sharp arrows resembling the flames of the fire of Time.
t.6.47.123: And this one whom you struck today with your spear, who, as if by his own wish, suddenly sank into despair, he, O king of the hosts of rākṣasas, is death today in battle for you, together with your sons and wives.
t.6.47.125: Though he was struck with arrows by the rākṣasa in battle, the splendour of that hero, endowed with innate brilliance, grew all the greater.
t.6.47.126: Then the mighty and splendid Rāma, seeing that tiger among monkeys wounded by Rāvaṇa, came under the sway of anger.
t.6.47.127: Advancing upon him, Rāma with his well-feathered arrows cut to pieces his chariot together with its wheels, its horses, banner, parasol and great flag, together with its charioteer, and together with its thunderbolts, spears and swords.
t.6.47.129: That king who had neither been shaken nor had wavered at the crashing fall of thunderbolts and lightning, that hero, struck by Rāma's arrows and sorely afflicted, now reeled and let fall his bow.
t.6.47.128: Then he swiftly struck the enemy of Indra with an arrow resembling the thunderbolt and the lightning, on his broad and beautifully formed chest, as the lord Indra struck Meru with his vajra.
t.6.47.130: Seeing him reeling, Rāma then took up a blazing crescent-headed arrow, and with it the great-souled one suddenly cut off the sun-coloured diadem of the lord of the Rākṣasas.
t.6.47.131: To him, the lord of the rākṣasas, who resembled a serpent bereft of its venom, who was like the sun with its rays quenched and its light gone dark, his splendour departed and the peak of his crown cut away, Rāma spoke in battle.
t.6.47.133: Thus addressed, the king, his pride and exultation destroyed, his bow cut to pieces, his horses and charioteer slain, tormented by arrows, his great crown cut off, swiftly entered Laṅkā.
t.6.47.132: A great and most terrible deed has been done by you, and by you I have been made one whose foremost heroes are slain. Therefore, judging that you are exhausted, I do not lead you into the power of death with my arrows.
t.6.47.134: When that mighty lord of the night-wanderers, the foe of the Dānavas and the gods, had entered the city, Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa freed the monkeys of their arrows at the forefront of that supreme battle.
t.6.47.135: When that foe of Indra, lord of the thirty gods, was routed, the gods and asuras, the hosts of beings and the quarters of the sky, together with the oceans, the seers and the great serpents, and likewise the creatures that move on land and in water, all rejoiced.
